Regression Models

Source: vignettes/regression-models.Rmd
regression-models.Rmd

Regression analyses of intensive longitudinal data can be conducted at three levels, each allowing a different degree of heterogeneity between persons (López-Pernas et al. 2025).

At the variable-centered (pooled) level, one model is estimated from the data of all persons together. The resulting coefficients describe the average association in the sample and assume that one set of coefficients adequately represents every person. At the person-centered (subgroup) level, the sample is partitioned into groups whose members share similar coefficient profiles, and one model is estimated for each group. At the person-specific (individual) level, a separate model is estimated for each person from that person’s own repeated measures. No similarity between persons is assumed, and many observations per person are required.

Question Function
What are the pooled and person-specific linear associations? fit_lm()
What are the pooled and person-specific binary or count associations? fit_glm()
Do within-person and between-person effects differ? fit_within_between()

The three functions accept a scope argument ("pooled", "subgroup", "individual", or any combination) and fit the selected levels on the same data, so that their coefficients can be compared directly.

fit_lm()

Analytic question

fit_lm() estimates a linear model at every requested scope and returns the results in one tidy object. The outcome, predictors, person identifier, and time column are specified once; the scope argument determines how many models are fitted. When scope = c("pooled", "individual"), both the pooled model and one model per person are estimated. Pooled and subgroup models combine the occasions of many persons, so their standard errors are cluster-robust (sandwich-estimated), clustered on the person identifier, rather than model-based. This ensures that the repeated occasions of the same person are not treated as independent observations.

Pooled and person-specific coefficients

The example below predicts daily effort from efficacy and monitoring for the 36 learners in the bundled srl data, each observed on 156 days.

lm_fit <- fit_lm(srl, y = "effort", x = c("efficacy", "monitoring"),
                 id = "name", time = "day",
                 scope = c("pooled", "individual"))
coefs(lm_fit, scope = "pooled")
#>    scope model estimator subject subgroup        term   estimate  std_error
#> 1 pooled    lm    native    .all     .all (Intercept) 27.9366297 4.64403728
#> 2 pooled    lm    native    .all     .all    efficacy  0.4415288 0.05638120
#> 3 pooled    lm    native    .all     .all  monitoring  0.1442609 0.04962956
#>   statistic      p_value
#> 1  6.015591 7.364519e-07
#> 2  7.831136 3.341992e-09
#> 3  2.906753 6.297403e-03

In the pooled model, estimated effort increased by 0.44 points per unit of efficacy (SE = 0.056) and by 0.14 points per unit of monitoring (SE = 0.050). Both standard errors are cluster-robust. Because every learner contributes to the same regression, these coefficients describe an average association that may not hold for any individual learner (López-Pernas et al. 2025).

Subgroup evidence

Whether the learners form distinct coefficient types is an empirical question. test_subgroups() compares Gaussian mixture models with one to four components by the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), where lower values indicate better fit. A one-component solution is a valid outcome of the comparison: it indicates that the coefficients are drawn from a single population rather than discrete types.

subgroup_test <- test_subgroups(srl, y = "effort",
                                x = c("efficacy", "monitoring"),
                                id = "name", time = "day")
subgroup_test
#> Idiographic Subgroup Test
#>   People:      36
#>   Coefficients: efficacy, monitoring
#>   Searched:    k = 1..4, covariance models EII/VII/EEI/VVI/EEE/VVV
#> 
#>   VERDICT:     no subgroups detected (one population fits best)
#>                Clustering these people anyway will still return
#>                groups -- they will not mean anything.
#> 
#>   Use as.data.frame() for the BIC table.
as.data.frame(subgroup_test) |> head()
#>   k model     loglik npar      bic selected
#> 1 1   EII -101.14942    3 213.0494     TRUE
#> 2 1   VII -101.14942    3 213.0494    FALSE
#> 3 1   EEI -101.14942    4 216.6329    FALSE
#> 4 1   VVI -101.14942    4 216.6329    FALSE
#> 5 2   EEI  -96.59769    7 218.2800    FALSE
#> 6 1   EEE -100.37905    5 218.6757    FALSE

The one-population model had the lowest BIC (213.0); the best two-component model reached 218.3. The learners therefore did not separate into subgroups, and a subgroup model would effectively reproduce the pooled model. The differences between learners were continuous, with no evidence of discrete types.

Person-specific coefficients

The individual scope returns one coefficient per learner. Sorting the efficacy slopes reveals the spread of person-specific associations.

The person-specific efficacy slopes ranged from -0.18 (Ravi) to 0.87 (Lars), with a median of 0.32. Seven of the 36 learners had negative slopes, and only eight had a slope within 0.10 of the pooled value of 0.44. The spread of these slopes contains both true between-person differences and sampling error, because each slope is estimated from a limited number of occasions.

Coefficient heterogeneity

pool_coefs() separates true heterogeneity from sampling error by fitting a DerSimonian–Laird random-effects model to the person-specific coefficients . The function reports the uncertainty-weighted pooled slope, the standard deviation of the true slopes (τ\tau), and the share of the observed spread attributable to true between-person differences (I2I^2).

pool_coefs(lm_fit)
#> POOLED PERSON EFFECTS
#>   Method   random effects (DerSimonian-Laird)
#>   People   36
#>   Terms    3
#> 
#>   term           k    pooled           95% CI   sd_obs      tau      I2      Q p
#> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#>   (Intercept)   36   31.9792   [22.59, 41.37]   23.432   27.054   0.968   <1e-04
#>   efficacy      36    0.2871     [0.20, 0.38]    0.271    0.252   0.912   <1e-04
#>   monitoring    36    0.1957     [0.09, 0.30]    0.299    0.276   0.919   <1e-04
#> 
#>   sd_obs = observed spread;  tau = spread of the true coefficients
#>   I2     = share of the observed spread that is real

For efficacy, the pooled slope was 0.29 (95% CI: 0.20 to 0.38), the estimated τ\tau was 0.25, and I2I^2 was 0.91. Under a normal approximation, the true slopes of 95% of learners lie between approximately $-$0.20 and 0.78 — a range that includes learners for whom efficacy is unrelated to effort. The pooling and shrinkage vignette covers pool_coefs() and shrink_coefs() in greater detail.

plot_coefs(lm_fit, term = "efficacy")

Figure 1. Person-specific efficacy slopes with 95% confidence intervals. The dashed line marks the pooled slope; the shaded band covers the interval expected to contain 95% of the true slopes.

fit_glm()

Analytic question

fit_glm() extends the same three-level framework to binary and count outcomes through a generalized linear model. The family argument accepts "binomial" for binary outcomes, "poisson" for counts, and "negbin" for overdispersed counts. Pooled and subgroup standard errors are again cluster-robust.

The bundled submissions data are simulated: 40 learners observed on 80 days, with a binary record of whether an assignment was submitted each day. The learners belong to two types. For the 20 engaged learners, the log-odds of submitting rise with daily motivation (true slope 1.2); for the 20 avoidant learners, they fall (true slope $-$0.6). Each learner’s slope varies slightly around the slope of the type, and the type column records the true type.

head(submissions)
#>   learner day    type motivation submitted
#> 1       1   1 engaged  1.3284155         1
#> 2       1   2 engaged  1.5540090         1
#> 3       1   3 engaged -0.3463324         0
#> 4       1   4 engaged  0.3191570         1
#> 5       1   5 engaged -2.3165814         0
#> 6       1   6 engaged -0.1089408         0

Pooled coefficients 

pooled_glm <- fit_glm(submissions, y = "submitted", x = "motivation",
                       id = "learner", family = "binomial",
                       time = "day", scope = "pooled")
coefs(pooled_glm)
#>    scope    model estimator subject subgroup        term   estimate  std_error
#> 1 pooled binomial    native    .all     .all (Intercept) -0.1210932 0.08797027
#> 2 pooled binomial    native    .all     .all  motivation  0.2297620 0.12060291
#>   statistic    p_value
#> 1 -1.376524 0.16865944
#> 2  1.905111 0.05676559

The pooled motivation slope was 0.23 (SE = 0.12, pp = .057). Averaged over both types, motivation appeared weakly related to submission — a coefficient that describes neither type of learner accurately. This is the expected consequence of pooling across processes with opposite signs.

Subgroup discovery

find_subgroups() first applies the mixture comparison internally (equivalent to test_subgroups()) and, when a multi-component representation is supported, assigns each learner to a group. Assignment stability is estimated through repeated resampling.

set.seed(1)
submission_groups <- find_subgroups(submissions, y = "submitted",
                                    x = "motivation", id = "learner",
                                    time = "day", k = "auto", reps = 30)
submission_groups
#> Idiographic Subgroups
#>   Method:      effect_clustering
#>   Subgroups:   2 (chosen automatically)
#>   People:      40
#>   Sizes:       g1=21, g2=19
#>   Stability:   0.92 (how reproducible the partition is --
#>                NOT evidence that the subgroups are real)
#> 
#>   VERDICT:     2 subgroups (mixture BIC beats one group by 23.9: very strong evidence)
#> 
#>   Use groups(), test_subgroups(), fit_subgroups()

Two subgroups were selected (BIC improvement of 23.9 over a single population). The partition coincided with the simulated types for 39 of the 40 learners. The subgroup assignment then enters fit_glm() through the subgroup argument, so that pooled, subgroup, and individual models are estimated together.

glm_fit <- fit_glm(submissions, y = "submitted", x = "motivation",
                    id = "learner", family = "binomial", time = "day",
                    scope = c("pooled", "subgroup", "individual"),
                    subgroup = submission_groups)
coefs(glm_fit, scope = "subgroup")
#>      scope    model estimator subject subgroup        term   estimate
#> 1 subgroup binomial    native    .all       g1 (Intercept) -0.2698968
#> 2 subgroup binomial    native    .all       g1  motivation -0.4353766
#> 3 subgroup binomial    native    .all       g2 (Intercept) -0.1201561
#> 4 subgroup binomial    native    .all       g2  motivation  1.1744905
#>    std_error statistic      p_value
#> 1 0.09741277 -2.770651 5.594442e-03
#> 2 0.10230837 -4.255533 2.085518e-05
#> 3 0.08109624 -1.481649 1.384338e-01
#> 4 0.06605776 17.779749 1.014329e-70

The subgroup motivation slopes were $-$0.44 and 1.17, close to the generating values of $-$0.6 and 1.2. The person-centered level recovered the two processes that the pooled coefficient had averaged away.

Coefficient heterogeneity 

pool_coefs(glm_fit)
#> POOLED PERSON EFFECTS
#>   Method   random effects (DerSimonian-Laird)
#>   People   40
#>   Terms    2
#> 
#>   term           k    pooled           95% CI   sd_obs     tau      I2       Q p
#> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#>   (Intercept)   40   -0.1641   [-0.30, -0.03]    0.423   0.261   0.409   0.00446
#>   motivation    40    0.2641    [-0.04, 0.57]    0.959   0.790   0.853   < 1e-04
#> 
#>   sd_obs = observed spread;  tau = spread of the true coefficients
#>   I2     = share of the observed spread that is real

The random-effects pooled motivation slope was 0.26 (95% CI: $-$0.04 to 0.57), the estimated τ\tau was 0.79, and I2I^2 was 0.85. The large τ\tau mainly reflects the distance between the two subgroups: the random-effects model describes the slopes with a single normal distribution, whereas the true generating distribution is bimodal.

plot_coefs(glm_fit, term = "motivation")

Figure 2. Person-specific motivation slopes with 95% confidence intervals. The dashed line marks the pooled slope; the shaded band covers the interval expected to contain 95% of the true slopes.

Assumptions and failure checks

Several conditions determine the validity of the results above.

  1. Independence of persons. Cluster-robust standard errors correct for within-person dependence but assume that persons are independent. Nested designs (learners within classrooms) require an additional clustering level.
  2. Sufficient occasions. Person-specific models require enough complete rows per person for estimation and for a meaningful held-out block. Persons with too few observations are recorded in the failure table rather than silently dropped.
  3. Outcome distribution. The binomial family assumes a binary outcome coded as 0/1 or as a two-level factor. Overdispersed counts should be modelled with "negbin" rather than "poisson", because the Poisson assumption of equal mean and variance produces standard errors that are too small when violated.
  4. Coefficient comparability. Pooling with pool_coefs() and subgroup discovery with find_subgroups() require person-specific coefficients that are on the same scale. Differing predictors, coding, or transformations across persons invalidate comparisons.

fit_within_between()

Analytic question

A regression on the raw scores of a repeated-measures variable conflates two associations: the association between a person’s daily deviations from their own average (within-person), and the association between persons’ long-run averages (between-person) (Saqr et al. 2024). Whether these two associations differ is an empirical question with substantive implications. A within-person effect of efficacy on effort describes how effort changes on days when efficacy is above or below a learner’s own typical level. A between-person effect describes whether learners who are generally more efficacious also tend to exert more effort.

fit_within_between() separates each predictor into its within-person and between-person parts — by person-mean centring the raw scores and including the person means as separate predictors — and estimates a slope for each part. The contextual() accessor reports both slopes and their difference, which indicates whether the between-person association exceeds (or falls short of) the within-person association.

Contextual effects 

wb_fit <- fit_within_between(srl, y = "effort",
                             x = c("efficacy", "monitoring"),
                             id = "name", time = "day")
contextual(wb_fit)
#>   variable     within   between   contextual     S.E.            95% CI        p
#> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#>   efficacy     0.3688    0.5862       0.2174   0.1015    [0.011, 0.423]   0.0392
#>   monitoring   0.1745    0.0978      -0.0767   0.0988   [-0.277, 0.124]   0.4427
#> 
#> scope = pooled,  model = within_between,  estimator = ols,  subject = .all,  subgroup = .all

For efficacy, the within-person slope was 0.37 and the between-person slope was 0.59. The difference of 0.22 (95% CI: 0.01 to 0.42, pp = .039) indicates a stronger association between learners than within them: learners who were generally more efficacious tended to exert disproportionately more effort than would be expected from the within-person relation alone. For monitoring, the within-person slope was 0.17 and the between-person slope was 0.10; the difference of $-$0.08 (95% CI: $-$0.28 to 0.12, pp = .44) was not distinguishable from zero.

Visualisation 

plot_components(wb_fit)

Figure 3. Within-person and between-person slopes with 95% confidence intervals.

Assumptions and failure checks

The decomposition requires that variation exists at both levels. A variable with no between-person variance (ICC near zero) has no between-person component to estimate; a variable constant within every person has no within-person component. The variance_components() function, described in the descriptives vignette, reports the ICC for each variable.

The contextual effect is an associational difference, not a causal estimate. The between-person slope is identified under the assumption that no time-invariant confounders jointly predict the outcome and the person-level predictor mean. When that assumption is untenable, the within-person slope remains identified under weaker conditions (no time-varying confounders), whereas the between-person slope and the contextual difference absorb unobserved between-person confounding.

Choice among the three functions

fit_lm() and fit_glm() estimate associations at pooled, subgroup, and individual levels. The choice between the two depends on the outcome distribution: continuous for fit_lm(), binary or count for fit_glm().

fit_within_between() separates within-person and between-person associations in the pooled regression. It addresses the question of whether the relation observed on days when a person deviates from their own average matches the relation observed across persons who differ in their averages. A substantial contextual effect indicates that the raw pooled coefficient is a weighted average of two different quantities.

Prediction accuracy at the individual level is examined in the prediction vignette with fit_ml(). Subgroup discovery and treatment-effect heterogeneity are covered in the subgroups and effects vignette with test_subgroups(), find_subgroups(), and fit_effects(). Coefficient synthesis and stabilisation are covered in the pooling and shrinkage vignette with pool_coefs() and shrink_coefs().
